subjects.title: CCAF 2 - Claude Code
subjects.description: Domain 2 (20%) - CLAUDE.md hierarchy, slash commands, hooks, permissions, headless mode, and CI/CD integration.

cards.question: List the CLAUDE.md scopes and explain how they combine.
cards.answer:
Four scopes, loaded from **broadest to most specific**:

| Scope | Location |
|---|---|
| **Managed policy** | `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md` (Linux/WSL), `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md` (macOS), `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md` (Windows) |
| **User** | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` - you, across every project |
| **Project** | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` - committed, team-shared |
| **Local** | `./CLAUDE.local.md` - your personal, gitignored project notes |

The critical detail: they are **concatenated into context, not overridden**. Everything discovered is present; the more specific file simply appears **later**, and later instructions carry more weight when they conflict. Claude Code also walks **up** the directory tree from the working directory, loading every `CLAUDE.md` it passes, and loads files in **subdirectories on demand** when it reads files there.

Managed policy CLAUDE.md cannot be excluded by user settings.
hints: Four locations. The verb that matters is concatenate, not override.

cards.question: A CLAUDE.md rule is being applied inconsistently. How do you diagnose and fix it?
cards.answer:
Work down four layers, in order:

1. **Is it even loaded?** Run **`/memory`** to see which memory files actually loaded this session. The most common cause is a rule sitting in **user-level** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` - which is not shared through version control, so a new teammate never receives it - when it belongs at **project level**.

2. **Is it drowning?** A large monolithic CLAUDE.md dilutes every instruction in it. Split it into topic-specific files under **`.claude/rules/`** (`testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`, `deployment.md`), or use **`@import`** to pull in only the standards each package needs.

3. **Is it relevant everywhere?** If it only applies to some files, path-scope it: a `.claude/rules/` file with YAML frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]` loads **only** when matching files are edited. Always-loaded universal standards stay in CLAUDE.md; everything else is on-demand.

4. **Does it need a guarantee?** Then it was never a memory file. Instructions have a non-zero failure rate; **programmatic enforcement** - a prerequisite gate, or a hook that intercepts the tool call - is what makes compliance deterministic.
hints: Start by proving it loaded at all. There is a command for exactly that.

cards.question: How do you create a custom slash command, and what does its frontmatter control?
cards.answer:
A markdown file whose **filename becomes the command name**, in one of two scopes:

- **`.claude/commands/review.md`** -> `/review`, **project-scoped**: shared with the team through version control.
- **`~/.claude/commands/review.md`** -> `/review`, **user-scoped**: personal, available in every project.

Subdirectories namespace it: `.claude/commands/git/sync.md` -> `/git:sync`.

The body is the prompt; `$ARGUMENTS` receives everything typed after the command name and `$1`, `$2` the positional arguments. Frontmatter tunes the rest:

```markdown
---
description: Review a PR against our checklist
argument-hint: <pr-number>
allowed-tools: Bash(gh pr view:*), Read, Grep
---
Review PR #$1. Check error handling, tests, and naming.
```

- **`argument-hint`** prompts the developer for the parameter when they invoke it bare.
- **`allowed-tools`** restricts tool access during execution - least privilege for this command only.

The same frontmatter options apply to **skills** in `.claude/skills/`, which also support `context: fork`.
hints: The filename names it. The frontmatter decides what it may touch.

cards.question: What do Agent SDK hooks do, and when do you choose one over a prompt instruction?
cards.answer:
Hooks intercept the tool-call cycle and run **your** code, outside the model's judgement. Two patterns the exam names:

- **`PostToolUse`** - intercept tool **results** and transform them **before the model processes them**. The canonical use is normalizing heterogeneous formats: one MCP tool returns Unix timestamps, another ISO 8601, a third numeric status codes. Normalize at the hook and the agent never has to reason about the difference.
- **Outgoing tool-call interception** - block a policy-violating action and redirect. Refund above $500? The hook blocks the call and routes it to the human escalation workflow.

When to choose a hook: **when the rule must hold every time**. A prompt instruction gives you probabilistic compliance - usually followed, with a non-zero failure rate. A hook gives you a deterministic guarantee, because the model is not in the enforcement path at all.

So: business rules, compliance limits, and data normalization are hooks. Style, tone, and preference are prompts.
hints: One pattern rewrites what comes back; the other blocks what goes out.

cards.question: How do you run Claude Code non-interactively for automation?
cards.answer:
**Headless mode**, with `-p` / `--print`: Claude runs the prompt, prints the result, and exits.

```bash
claude -p "Review the staged diff and list blocking issues" \
  --output-format json \
  --allowedTools "Read,Grep,Bash(git diff:*)" \
  --permission-mode acceptEdits
```

Key flags:
- `--output-format` - `text` (default), `json` (one result object with cost and session id), or `stream-json` (events as they happen).
- `--allowedTools` / `--disallowedTools` - the permission surface for this run.
- `--permission-mode` - e.g. `plan`, `acceptEdits`.
- `--append-system-prompt` - inject instructions at the system-prompt level.
- `--resume <session-id>` / `--continue` - keep going from a previous run.

Headless mode **does not persist between runs** unless you resume a session, and it is the building block for CI jobs, git hooks, and batch scripts. Never use `--dangerously-skip-permissions` outside an isolated container.
hints: One flag makes it a one-shot command; another makes the output parseable by the next step.

cards.question: How are MCP servers scoped in Claude Code, and how do credentials stay out of git?
hints: One file is committed, one is yours. Both load at the same time.

cards.question: What lives in the `.claude/` directory, and what decides which file a given instruction goes in?
cards.answer:
```text
.claude/
├── CLAUDE.md      # always-loaded universal standards (or root CLAUDE.md)
├── rules/         # topic files; YAML `paths` globs load them conditionally
├── commands/      # slash commands, project-scoped via version control
├── skills/        # SKILL.md + assets, loaded on demand
└── agents/        # subagent definitions: description, prompt, tool limits
```

Plus **`.mcp.json`** at the repo root for shared servers, and **`~/.claude.json`** outside the repo for your personal ones.

The routing question is **how often the instruction is relevant**:

| Relevance | Home |
|---|---|
| Every session, universal | `CLAUDE.md` |
| Only when editing matching files | `rules/` with a `paths` glob |
| Only when a specific task comes up | `skills/` |
| Only when a developer asks for it by name | `commands/` |

Path-scoped rules beat a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md` when the convention follows a **file type** rather than a directory - test files spread across the whole tree are the standard example.
hints: Sort the whole directory by one question: how often does this matter?

cards.question: What is the `@path` import syntax in CLAUDE.md and what is its limit?
cards.answer:
A CLAUDE.md can pull in other files with `@path/to/file`:

```markdown
See @README.md for the overview and @docs/git-workflow.md for branching rules.
```

Relative paths resolve against the **file containing the import**, not the working directory. Absolute paths and `~/` work too. Imported files can import further files, up to a maximum depth of **four hops**.

Two details that get tested:
- Import parsing **skips code spans and fenced code blocks**, so writing `` `@README` `` in backticks mentions the path without importing it.
- Imports **do not save context** - imported files are expanded and loaded at launch just like inline text. They are for organization. To actually reduce context, use **path-scoped rules** in `.claude/rules/` (loaded only when Claude touches matching files) or **skills** (loaded on demand).
hints: There is a hop limit - and a very common belief about context savings that is wrong.

cards.question: How do you define a custom subagent in Claude Code and why would you?
cards.answer:
A markdown file with YAML frontmatter in `.claude/agents/` (project) or `~/.claude/agents/` (personal):

```markdown
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Reviews a diff for security issues. Use after changes to auth or input handling.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: opus
---
You are a security reviewer. Focus on injection, authz, and secret handling.
Return findings as a list of file:line + severity + fix.
```

Why: **context isolation** (it works in its own window and returns a short result), **specialization** (a narrower system prompt beats a general one), **least privilege** (a reviewer gets no write tools), and **parallelism** (independent subagents run concurrently).

The `description` matters most - it is what the main agent reads to decide when to delegate. Write it as a trigger condition, not a title.
hints: A markdown file with frontmatter, where one field decides when it actually gets used.

cards.question: Your CLAUDE.md has grown to 600 lines and adherence is getting worse. What do you do?
cards.answer:
Long files consume context on every session and **reduce** adherence; the guidance is to target **under 200 lines**. Fixes, in order of value:

1. **Move path-scoped content to `.claude/rules/`** with `paths` frontmatter, so it loads only when Claude touches matching files:
   ```markdown
   ---
   paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"]
   ---
   All endpoints validate input with Zod.
   ```
2. **Move multi-step procedures to skills**, which load on demand instead of every session.
3. **Delete what Claude can derive** from the codebase - directory listings, dependency lists, architecture recaps. Keep pitfalls, rationale, and conventions that differ from the tool defaults.
4. **Remove contradictions**, including in ancestor and nested CLAUDE.md files.

What does **not** help: splitting into `@` imports. Imported files still load in full at launch, so the context cost is unchanged - only the file organization improves.
hints: Imports will not help. What actually loads on demand instead of at launch?

cards.question: Three MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and numeric codes, and the agent keeps comparing them wrongly. What is the cleanest fix?
cards.answer: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results for transformation before the model sees them, which is exactly the named use case for normalizing heterogeneous formats. Rewriting third-party servers is often not available to you; prompting makes the model do arithmetic it should never have been handed.

choices.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes each tool's result before the model processes it
A system prompt section explaining each tool's date format and how to convert between them
Few-shot examples showing correct date comparisons across all three of the tool formats
A rewrite of the three MCP servers so every one of them emits ISO 8601 timestamps

hints: Fix it once on the way in, or explain it forever in the prompt?

cards.question: You have a user `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and a project `./CLAUDE.md`. How does Claude Code combine them?
cards.answer: Both are concatenated into context, ordered broad to specific, so the project file appears after the user file and carries more weight on conflicts. CLAUDE.md files do not override each other the way settings files do.

choices.text: Both load; the project file appears later in context and wins on conflicts
The project file replaces the user file entirely for work in this repository
The user file wins, because user-level configuration outranks project scope
Only the file nearest the working directory loads; the other is ignored entirely

hints: Do CLAUDE.md files replace one another, or pile up?

cards.question: A CI job must have Claude review every PR and emit machine-readable output for a downstream step. What is the right invocation?
cards.answer: Headless mode with `--print` and `--output-format json` gives a single structured result object the next step can parse. The `@claude` mention flow is interactive and only fires when a human writes a comment.

choices.text: `claude -p "..." --output-format json` with an explicit `--allowedTools` list
An interactive `claude` session in the runner
Post an `@claude` comment from the workflow and wait
`claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` so nothing blocks the run

hints: "Every PR" eliminates one option; "machine-readable" eliminates another.

cards.question: Where do you put an MCP server config so the whole team gets it from version control?
cards.answer: `.mcp.json` at the repository root is the project scope - committed and shared. Claude Code asks for approval before using servers defined there, since it is configuration authored by other people.

choices.text: `.mcp.json` at the repository root
`~/.claude/settings.json`
`.claude/settings.local.json`
`CLAUDE.md`, as a documented setup step

hints: Version control means a committed file - and this one does not live inside .claude/.

cards.question: A file at `.claude/commands/deploy/staging.md` creates which slash command?
cards.answer: `/deploy:staging` - subdirectories namespace commands, and the filename is the command name.

choices.text: `/deploy:staging`
`/staging`
`/deploy/staging`
`/deploy staging`

hints: Subdirectories do something specific to the command name.

cards.question: Which skill frontmatter field prompts the developer for a parameter when the skill is invoked bare?
cards.answer: `argument-hint` supplies the expected-parameter hint shown when a developer invokes the skill without arguments. `allowed-tools` restricts tools, `context: fork` runs it in an isolated subagent, and `description` drives when Claude loads it.

choices.text: `argument-hint`
`allowed-tools`
`context: fork`
`description`

hints: The name says what it hints at.

cards.question: Your CLAUDE.md is too long. Which change actually reduces the context it consumes?
cards.answer: Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with matching files, so they genuinely cut startup context. `@` imports are expanded and loaded at launch, so they reorganize without saving anything.

choices.text: Move sections into `.claude/rules/` files with `paths` frontmatter
Split it into several files pulled in with `@path` imports
Move the content into `CLAUDE.local.md`
Wrap the long sections in HTML comments

hints: Which option actually loads less at startup, rather than just reorganizing the files?

cards.question: What is the most important field in a custom subagent definition for getting it used at the right time?
cards.answer: `description`. The main agent reads it to decide whether to delegate, so it should read as a trigger condition ("use after changes to auth or input handling"), not as a title.

choices.text: `description` - it is what the main agent matches against to decide when to delegate
`model` - it decides the capability tier the subagent will run at
`name` - the main agent matches the task against the subagent's name
`tools` - without an explicit tool list the subagent cannot act on anything at all

hints: The main agent has to decide to delegate. What does it read in order to decide?

cards.question: Which file name holds a project's committed, team-shared Claude Code instructions?
cards.answer: `CLAUDE.md`, at the repo root or in `.claude/`. `CLAUDE.local.md` is the gitignored personal variant.
hints: All caps, dot md - it sits at the repo root or inside .claude/.

cards.question: Which CLI flag runs Claude Code non-interactively for scripting (short form)?
cards.answer: `-p` (long form `--print`). Combine with `--output-format json` for machine-readable results.
hints: A single letter - short for print.

cards.question: Which file at the repository root defines MCP servers shared with the whole team?
cards.answer: `.mcp.json`. Claude Code prompts for approval before using servers declared there.
hints: A dotfile at the repo root, named after the protocol itself.

cards.question: Which directory inside `.claude/` holds custom slash commands?
cards.answer: `commands/` - each `.md` file becomes a command named after the file.
hints: Plural, and it is what you type after a leading slash.

cards.question: Which slash command shows which memory files actually loaded into the current session?
cards.answer: `/context`. Check the **Memory files** section - if your CLAUDE.md is not listed, Claude cannot see it.
hints: It shows you what is in the window right now.

cards.question: Match each CLAUDE.md scope to its location.
cards.answer: Load order runs broadest to most specific, and all of them are concatenated rather than overriding each other.
hints: Order them by breadth: the whole machine, then you everywhere, then the team, then just you here.

cards.question: Match each requirement to the Claude Code mechanism that satisfies it.
cards.answer: The recurring split: `CLAUDE.md` is always-loaded context, `rules/` is conditionally-loaded context, skills are on-demand workflows, and tool restrictions are the only thing that actually prevents an action.

matchPairs.left: Conventions for test files spread across the tree
A verbose analysis that must not pollute the session
Universal standards needed in every session
Diagnosing why an instruction never applied
Stopping a subagent from editing any file

hints: Sort into always loaded, conditionally loaded, on demand, and actually enforced.

cards.question: A new team member does not get the conventions everyone else's Claude follows. Where is the problem?
cards.answer: User-level settings apply only to that user - instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are not shared with teammates via version control. Diagnosing this is a named skill, and the fix is moving them to project level.

choices.text: The instructions sit in user-level `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is not shared through git
The instructions sit in the project `CLAUDE.md`, which they have not pulled yet
Their Claude Code version predates the configuration hierarchy the team relies on
The instructions use `@import`, and the imported files are missing on their machine

hints: Whose machine is that file on?

cards.question: A monorepo has eight packages with different standards, and one CLAUDE.md is becoming unmanageable. What does the guide suggest?
cards.answer: The @import syntax references external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular - selectively including the standards files relevant to each package. Duplication drifts; prefixing keeps everything loaded for everyone.

choices.text: Use `@import` so each package's CLAUDE.md pulls in only the standards files it needs
Duplicate the relevant sections into a CLAUDE.md inside each of the eight packages
Keep one CLAUDE.md and prefix each rule with the package name it applies to
Move all eight sets of standards into skills, invoked per package on demand

hints: One file per standard, imported where it applies.

cards.question: Which directory holds topic-specific rule files as an alternative to a monolithic CLAUDE.md?
cards.answer: `.claude/rules/` - files like `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`, `deployment.md`, each of which can be path-scoped with YAML frontmatter so it loads only when relevant.
hints: It sits next to commands/ and skills/.

cards.question: How do path-specific rules work, and when do they beat a subdirectory CLAUDE.md?
cards.answer:
A file in **`.claude/rules/`** with **YAML frontmatter containing a `paths` field of glob
patterns**:

```markdown
---
paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
---
Always pin provider versions. Never inline a secret; reference the vault data source.
```

The rule **loads only when files matching the glob are being edited**. Two consequences: irrelevant
context stays out of the window, and token usage drops for every session that never touches those
files.

**When it beats a subdirectory `CLAUDE.md`**: when the convention follows a **file type** rather
than a **location**. The canonical example is test files - `**/*.test.tsx` matches them wherever
they live, and they are typically spread across the whole tree. A directory-level CLAUDE.md would
have to be created in every directory that contains tests, and maintained as new ones appear.

So the discriminator is one question: **is this convention about where the file is, or about what
kind of file it is?**

| Convention scoped by | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| A directory (`packages/api/`) | Subdirectory CLAUDE.md, or `paths` glob on that directory |
| A file type, anywhere | `.claude/rules/` with a `paths` glob |
| Everything, always | Project CLAUDE.md |
hints: Location or file type? That is the whole decision.

cards.question: Terraform conventions should load only when Terraform files are being edited. What do you write?
cards.answer: Path-scoped rules with YAML frontmatter glob patterns load only when matching files are edited, which reduces irrelevant context and token usage. A directory CLAUDE.md is a reasonable second choice here, but the glob generalizes to files outside that directory.

choices.text: A `.claude/rules/` file with frontmatter `paths: ["terraform/**/*"]`
A `CLAUDE.md` inside the terraform directory describing those conventions
A project `CLAUDE.md` section that opens by naming the files it applies to
A skill named terraform-conventions that Claude loads when it detects the files

hints: There is a frontmatter field whose whole job is this.

cards.question: What do the skill frontmatter options do, and how do you choose between a skill and CLAUDE.md?
cards.answer:
A skill is a `SKILL.md` in **`.claude/skills/`** (project-scoped, shared through version
control) or **`~/.claude/skills/`** (personal). Its frontmatter carries three options that matter:

- **`context: fork`** - run the skill in an **isolated sub-agent context**, so its output does not
  pollute the main conversation. Use it for anything verbose (codebase analysis) or exploratory
  (brainstorming alternatives) - the noise happens elsewhere and only the conclusion returns.
- **`allowed-tools`** - restrict tool access **during skill execution**. Least privilege for this
  one workflow: limit to file writes and a destructive command becomes unavailable regardless of
  what the skill's prose says.
- **`argument-hint`** - prompt the developer for required parameters when they invoke the skill
  without arguments, instead of the skill guessing or failing.

**Skill or CLAUDE.md?** By **how often it is relevant**:

- **CLAUDE.md** - always-loaded **universal standards**. Every session pays for it, so it must earn
  that.
- **Skill** - **on-demand invocation for task-specific workflows**. A twenty-step deployment
  procedure used monthly costs nothing on the sessions that do not deploy.

**Personal customization without disrupting the team**: create a variant in `~/.claude/skills/`
with a **different name**. Same name would shadow the shared one and quietly diverge your
behaviour from everyone else's.
hints: Three frontmatter options: one isolates, one restricts, one asks.

cards.question: A codebase-analysis skill floods the main conversation with file listings before the real work starts. What fixes it?
cards.answer: context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing skill outputs from polluting the main conversation. Compacting afterwards recovers space but the main session already spent it, and restricting tools does not make discovery quiet.

choices.text: Add `context: fork` so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context
Add `allowed-tools` limiting the skill to Read so it produces less output overall
Move the skill body into a separate file the skill reads only when it needs to
Run `/compact` after the skill finishes, reclaiming the space its output consumed

hints: Do not clean it up afterwards - have it happen somewhere else.

cards.question: You want a personal variant of a shared team skill, without affecting teammates. How?
cards.answer: Personal skill customization means creating variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names, to avoid affecting teammates. Reusing the name shadows the shared skill and silently diverges your behaviour from the team's.

choices.text: Create it in `~/.claude/skills/` under a different name
Create it in `~/.claude/skills/` with the same name, so yours takes precedence
Edit the project skill and add a note that the change is a personal preference
Copy it into `.claude/skills/` with a suffix, then gitignore that one file

hints: Personal scope is half of it. The other half is the name.

cards.question: Which skill frontmatter option runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context?
cards.answer: `context: fork`. It keeps verbose or exploratory skill output out of the main conversation, returning only what the session needs.
hints: A key and a value, and the value is a git word.

cards.question: Match each configuration surface to what belongs in it.
cards.answer: The organizing question is frequency and audience: always or sometimes, everyone or just you. Getting the last row wrong is the named cause of a teammate never receiving a convention.

matchPairs.right: Conventions for one file type, wherever it lives
A prompt a developer invokes by name
Your own preference, on every project, shared with nobody

hints: Two axes: how often it matters, and who gets it.

cards.question: When is plan mode the right choice, and what is the Explore subagent for?
cards.answer:
**Plan mode** is for tasks with **large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches,
architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications**. It lets the codebase be explored and the
design settled **before** committing to changes, which is what prevents costly rework.

**Direct execution** is for simple, well-scoped work: a single-file bug fix with a clear stack
trace, adding one validation conditional.

Concrete calls from the guide:

| Task | Mode |
|---|---|
| Microservice restructuring | Plan |
| A library migration touching 45+ files | Plan |
| Choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure | Plan |
| Single-file fix with a clear stack trace | Direct |
| Adding a date validation conditional | Direct |

**They compose.** Plan the library migration, then execute the planned approach directly - the
question is rarely which one for the whole task, but which one for the phase you are in.

**The Explore subagent** solves the adjacent problem: discovery is verbose, and a multi-phase task
can exhaust its context window on file listings and greps before reaching the work. Explore
isolates the discovery phase and **returns summaries**, preserving the main conversation's context
for the actual task.
hints: Count the files and count the viable approaches. Either number being high decides it.

cards.question: A stack trace points at one function and the fix is a missing null check. Plan mode or direct execution?
cards.answer: Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes - a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace is the guide's own example. Plan mode is for large-scale change, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions.

choices.text: Direct execution - the scope is clear and the change is contained
Plan mode, because any production fix deserves a reviewed plan first
Plan mode, since the null check may reveal other unguarded call sites
Direct execution, but only after Explore has mapped the calling code

hints: One file, one line, one clear cause.

cards.question: A multi-phase task keeps running out of context during its discovery phase. What is the mechanism for that?
cards.answer: The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries, preserving main conversation context - which is exactly what prevents context exhaustion during multi-phase tasks. Compacting is a recovery, not a preventive.

choices.text: The Explore subagent, which isolates discovery and returns summaries
Plan mode, which defers all file reading until the plan has been approved
A skill with `allowed-tools` restricted to Read, keeping the discovery narrow
Running `/compact` between the discovery phase and the implementation phase

hints: Have the noisy part happen in someone else's window.

cards.question: What are the iterative refinement techniques, and when does each apply?
cards.answer:
Four techniques, each with a trigger:

**1. Concrete input/output examples** - when a prose description is being interpreted
inconsistently. Two or three examples of the actual transformation communicate what paragraphs of
description cannot. This is the first thing to reach for when "it keeps doing it slightly
differently".

**2. Test-driven iteration** - write the test suite **first**, covering expected behaviour, edge
cases, and performance requirements; then iterate by **sharing the failures**. The failing test is
a precise, machine-generated description of the gap.

**3. The interview pattern** - have Claude **ask questions** to surface considerations you have not
thought of, **before** implementing. The value is highest in unfamiliar domains: it raises cache
invalidation strategies and failure modes while they are still cheap to address.

**4. Batched versus sequential fixes** - and this one has a real rule:

- **Interacting** problems go in **one detailed message**, because fixing them separately means
  each fix invalidates the last.
- **Independent** problems go **sequentially**, one at a time, so each change is verifiable.

Getting that backwards is a common waste: batching independent issues makes it unclear which change
caused what, and sequencing interacting issues sends you round in circles.
hints: Four techniques, and the last one is a rule about grouping, not about wording.

cards.question: A prose description of a data transformation keeps being implemented slightly differently. What is the most effective fix?
cards.answer: Concrete input/output examples are named as the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. More prose - even better organized prose - is still prose.

choices.text: Provide two or three concrete input/output examples of the transformation
Rewrite the description as a numbered procedure with one action per step
Add the edge cases to the description, since those are where it diverges
Ask for the implementation plan first, then correct it before any code

hints: Stop describing it and show it.

cards.question: You have five review findings, and fixing any one of them changes how the others should be fixed. How do you send them?
cards.answer: Interacting problems go in one message; independent problems are better fixed sequentially. Sequential iteration on interacting fixes means each one invalidates the previous.

choices.text: All five in a single detailed message, since the fixes interact
One at a time, verifying each fix before moving on to the next finding
Grouped by file, so each message keeps its changes locally consistent
Highest severity first, alone, then the remaining four together afterwards

hints: They interact. What does fixing one in isolation do to the others?

cards.question: What is the name of the technique where Claude asks questions to surface considerations before implementing?
cards.answer: The interview pattern. Most valuable in unfamiliar domains, where it raises things like cache invalidation strategy and failure modes before they are expensive.
hints: It is named after a conversation where one side asks all the questions.

cards.question: A CI review re-runs after each new commit and the PR is filling with duplicate comments. What fixes it?
cards.answer: Including prior review findings in context and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues is the named skill. Reviewing only the newest commit misses issues introduced by the interaction between commits.

choices.text: Include the prior findings and ask for only new or still-unaddressed issues
Delete the previous comments before each run so only the latest set remains
Run the review only on the newest commit's diff rather than the full branch
Deduplicate the findings in the posting step by comparing their text content

hints: The agent does not know what it already said unless you tell it.

cards.question: Generated tests keep duplicating scenarios the suite already covers. What is missing from the invocation?
cards.answer: Providing existing test files in context is what stops duplicate scenarios, and documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md is what reduces low-value test output.

choices.text: The existing test files, plus documented fixtures and test criteria in CLAUDE.md
A higher turn limit, so the agent can read the suite before writing anything
A stricter prompt telling the agent not to duplicate any existing test case
A coverage report, so the agent writes tests only for the uncovered lines

hints: It cannot avoid what it has not seen.

cards.question: Which CLI flag pairs with `--output-format json` to enforce the shape of CI output?
cards.answer: `--json-schema`. Together they produce machine-parseable structured findings a later pipeline step can post as inline PR comments.
hints: Two dashes, then the thing you want the output to obey.
